Global Exponential Convergence
of Two-Layer Linear Network Training

Stephen Zhang Affiliation: Flatiron Institute & NYU Email: syz@syz.id.au    Gabriel Peyré Affiliation: CNRS, ENS, PSL Univ. Email: gabriel.peyre@ens.fr
Abstract

We prove global exponential (linear) convergence with an explicit rate in the rich scaling for wide two-layer linear networks trained with smooth Polyak–Łojasiewicz predictor losses. Gradient flow in the factors closes exactly in terms of a finite-dimensional Bures flow of the neuron law covariance, in which the predictor dynamics are preconditioned by hidden covariance blocks. Mean-field conservation laws provide uniform spectral lower bounds on the hidden preconditioning blocks when the initial covariance satisfies a spectral support gap condition. This condition encompasses positive definiteness while still allowing for singular initializations. For an initial covariance Σ0=σ2​Id\Sigma_{0}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}, the loss converges to the global minimum with linear rate at least 4​σ2​κ4\sigma^{2}\kappa, where κ\kappa is the PL constant. We establish stability of this rate under finite-width sampling, as well as global convergence of factor gradient descent for an explicit stepsize interval depending on smoothness, the initial loss, and conserved spectral margins. Our argument extends layerwise to deep linear ResNets, subject to a residual-path bound. In the case of heavy-ball momentum, training dynamics close instead over positions and velocities in terms of a lifted phase covariance. Linear convergence holds under an explicit condition on the energy and damping, specifying a window of admissible dampings. For two-scale white initializations, this interval is nonempty for sufficiently large position scales, with a fixed initial loss gap and velocity covariance. Numerical experiments illustrate the covariance geometry and compare the predicted and observed rates.

1 Introduction

Two-layer linear networks are nonconvex in their weight factors, even when the loss is a simple function of the predictor matrix. Training moves in the lifted space of incoming and outgoing neuron weights, whose second moments act as a time-dependent preconditioner on the predictor. These moments may in principle become degenerate and slow down the dynamics, and it is not clear that the dynamics necessarily converge to a globally optimal predictor. We consider this question in the rich mean-field scaling, in which both sides of each rank-one neuron evolve, and smooth predictor losses satisfying a Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality, which subsume the standard quadratic loss.

Central to our analysis are width-independent conservation laws for the weight covariance: the signed covariance spectrum, relative to the input-output block split, supplies conserved supporting inequalities and lower bounds on each hidden-block. The sum of these lower bounds conditions the predictor dynamics: a positive sum is sufficient to guarantee global convergence of the predictor loss with an explicit rate. This analysis covers every positive-definite initialization and some singular ones. For initial variance σ2​Id\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}, the loss decays with rate at least 4​σ2​κ4\sigma^{2}\kappa, where κ\kappa is the PL constant.

The covariance viewpoint also makes the result robust to finite-width sampling and factor gradient descent. For deep linear ResNets, the same conservation argument applied layerwise yields linear convergence conditional on a uniform bound on the residual path. With heavy-ball momentum, closure is lifted to the joint phase covariance of positions and velocities. Conformally transported spectral laws describe its geometry, while energy dissipation gives an explicit initialization and damping certificate for linear convergence. Special values of the conserved quantities further permit lower-dimensional intrinsic dynamics; these reductions are described in Appendix E.

Related work

Mean-field analyses describe the collective evolution of neuron weight distributions in wide two-layer networks (Chizat and Bach, 2018; Mei et al., 2018; Rotskoff and Vanden-Eijnden, 2018). These formulations treat broad nonlinear feature maps and often prove asymptotic global optimality or propagation-of-chaos type statements under support, homogeneity, noise, or regularity assumptions. In the present linear setting, exact second-moment closure connects training to Bures–Wasserstein covariance geometry (Takatsu, 2011; Bhatia et al., 2019), making a sharp quantitative linear convergence rate available. This closure distinguishes our analysis from the NTK (Jacot et al., 2018) and lazy training (Chizat et al., 2019) regime: both incoming and outgoing weights move, and the evolving representation is essential to the rate.

Deep linear networks have served as a tractable model of the nonconvexity created by matrix products, with results on their landscapes, exact dynamics, and convergence (Saxe et al., 2014; Kawaguchi, 2016; Laurent and von Brecht, 2018; Arora et al., 2019). Finite-width analyses of two-layer matrix factorization furnish convergence guarantees under small, asymmetric, or general initializations (Ye and Du, 2021; Xu et al., 2023), while recent work treats discrete-time low-rank adaptation directly (Mu and Klabjan, 2026). Our result instead starts from a population covariance satisfying a positive support gap condition, in particular any positive-definite covariance, and obtains an explicit global rate that survives independent finite-width sampling. Related work identifies Gramian differences and balancedness as invariants of factor training (Du et al., 2018; Tarmoun et al., 2021) and develops a general differential framework for identifying conservation laws (Marcotte et al., 2023). Our mean-field laws are functionals of the neuron distribution that induce compatible particle laws at every width. The conserved spectrum of the signed covariance yields hidden-block lower bounds without requiring a special balancedness identity.

Residual networks (He et al., 2016a; He et al., 2016b) were introduced as architectures built from perturbations of the identity, and their infinite depth limit leads naturally to neural ODEs (He et al., 2016a; Chen et al., 2018). Mean-field formulations have established global optimality and convergence results under expressivity, regularity, or local PL conditions (Lu et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021; Isobe, 2023; Barboni et al., 2025). Our linear analysis provides a complementary condition: uniform conditioning of the forward and backward residual products is sufficient for convergence.

Momentum turns first-order descent into an inertial, second-order iteration; the heavy-ball method of Polyak (1964) and Nesterov acceleration (Nesterov, 1983) have mature convergence theories, including continuous-time interpretations (Su et al., 2016) and robust-control analyses (Lessard et al., 2016). For deep linear networks, Wang et al. (2021); Liu et al. (2022) establish acceleration results under initialization and overparameterization conditions. Here the appropriate state variable is the phase covariance, over which the dynamics close. We give an explicit energy-damping certificate for global convergence with general position-velocity correlations.

Our contributions

Section 2 identifies width-independent spectral conservation laws and derives uniform hidden-block bounds from their support margins (Propositions 2.1 and 2.3). Their Wasserstein interpretation and local completeness among smooth covariance laws common to all split losses are developed in Appendices B and D. Section 3 proves global exponential convergence with an explicit rate under a smooth PL predictor loss from every initial covariance with positive support gap (Theorem 3.1). The rate survives independent finite-width sampling at width proportional to the population covariance rank, which can be as small as min⁡(du,dv)\min(d_{u},d_{v}) (Corollary 3.4 and Remark 3.5). We establish global linear convergence of factor gradient descent under an explicit stepsize bound by controlling the accumulated conservation error (Theorem 3.6). Section 4 extends the layerwise argument to finite- and continuous-depth linear ResNets under residual-path control (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2), and discusses why that control is not automatic (Remark C.19 in Appendix C.6). Section 5 shows that heavy-ball momentum dynamics closes on the phase covariance and identifies conformal conservation laws (Proposition 5.1). Global exponential convergence is proven under an initial-energy and damping condition, including a two-scale white specialization (Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3). A computational toolbox, code reproducing all six article figures, and illustrative Jupyter notebooks are available at https://github.com/gpeyre/linear-networks-global.

Setup

Writing training in terms of the predictor separates the loss geometry from the nonconvex factorization. A width-nn two-layer linear network has factors U:=(u1,…,un)∈ℝdu×nU:=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}\times n} and V:=(v1,…,vn)∈ℝdv×nV:=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times n}. Write m:=du+dvm:=d_{u}+d_{v} and W:=(UV)W:=\binom{U}{V}. Its predictor is Σv​u:=V​U⊤/n\Sigma^{vu}:=VU^{\top}/n, and its factor objective is ℒ⁡(U,V):=ℓ⁡(V​U⊤/n)\mathcal{L}(U,V):=\ell(VU^{\top}/n) for a differentiable predictor loss ℓ:ℝdv×du→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}}\to\mathbb{R}. For example, if a data distribution ρ\rho on pairs (z,y)(z,y) satisfies y=Σ⋆v​u​zy=\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}z for a teacher Σ⋆v​u\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}, squared regression loss is

ℓquad​(Σv​u):=12​∫‖(Σv​u−Σ⋆v​u)​z‖2​𝑑ρ​(z,y).\textstyle\ell_{\rm quad}(\Sigma^{vu}):=\frac{1}{2}\int\left\lVert(\Sigma^{vu}-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star})z\right\rVert^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\rho(z,y).

More generally, a self-adjoint positive semidefinite operator 𝒬\mathcal{Q} on ℝdv×du\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}} defines a quadratic loss ℓ⁡(S):=12​⟨𝒬⁡[S−Σ⋆v​u],S−Σ⋆v​u⟩\ell(S):=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\mathcal{Q}[S-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}],S-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}\right\rangle. The regression example corresponds to 𝒬⁡[X]=X​Cz\mathcal{Q}[X]=XC_{z}, where Cz:=∫z​z⊤​𝑑ρ​(z,y)C_{z}:=\int zz^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}\rho(z,y) is the input second moment.

We state the assumptions on the predictor loss: assume throughout that ℓ:ℝdv×du→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}}\to\mathbb{R} is C1C^{1} and bounded below, and write ℓ⋆:=infSℓ⁡(S)\ell_{\star}:=\inf_{S}\ell(S).

Assumption 1.1 (Smooth PL predictor loss).

There exist constants L>0L>0 and κ>0\kappa>0 such that the loss ℓ\ell is LL-smooth and satisfies the κ\kappa-Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality: ‖∇ℓ​(S)−∇ℓ​(S′)‖F≤L​‖S−S′‖F\left\lVert\nabla\ell(S)-\nabla\ell(S^{\prime})\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\leq L\left\lVert S-S^{\prime}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} for all S,S′S,S^{\prime}, and ‖∇ℓ​(S)‖F2≥2​κ​(ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆)\left\lVert\nabla\ell(S)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\geq 2\kappa\bigl(\ell(S)-\ell_{\star}\bigr) for all SS.

We take 0<κ≤L0<\kappa\leq L, as holds automatically for any nonconstant loss satisfying Assumption 1.1. For a nonzero quadratic Hessian 𝒬⪰0\mathcal{Q}\succeq 0, one can take L=λmax​(𝒬)L=\lambda_{\max}(\mathcal{Q}) and κ=λmin+​(𝒬)\kappa=\lambda_{\min}^{+}(\mathcal{Q}). The operator 𝒬\mathcal{Q} may have a nontrivial kernel.

2 Mean-field conservation laws

Gradient flow and covariance closure

Although training evolves all neuron weights, its effect on the predictor is governed by a fixed-size covariance matrix. We use the width-normalized gradient flow (U˙t,V˙t)=−n​∇(U,V)ℒ​(Ut,Vt)(\dot{U}_{t},\dot{V}_{t})=-n\nabla_{(U,V)}\mathcal{L}(U_{t},V_{t}), namely

U˙t=−Et⊤​Vt,V˙t=−Et​Ut,Et:=∇ℓ​(Vt​Ut⊤/n).\dot{U}_{t}=-E_{t}^{\top}V_{t},\qquad\dot{V}_{t}=-E_{t}U_{t},\qquad E_{t}:=\nabla\ell(V_{t}U_{t}^{\top}/n). (1)

The factor nn fixes a common time scale across widths; equivalently this is Euclidean gradient flow of n​ℒn\mathcal{L}. With Wt:=(UtVt)W_{t}:=\binom{U_{t}}{V_{t}}, define the uncentered covariance

Σt:=1n​Wt​Wt⊤=(ΣtuΣtu​vΣtv​uΣtv),Σtu:=Ut​Ut⊤n,Σtv:=Vt​Vt⊤n,Σtv​u:=Vt​Ut⊤n.\Sigma_{t}:=\tfrac{1}{n}W_{t}W_{t}^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma^{u}_{t}&\Sigma^{uv}_{t}\\ \Sigma^{vu}_{t}&\Sigma^{v}_{t}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Sigma^{u}_{t}:=\tfrac{U_{t}U_{t}^{\top}}{n},\quad\Sigma^{v}_{t}:=\tfrac{V_{t}V_{t}^{\top}}{n},\quad\Sigma^{vu}_{t}:=\tfrac{V_{t}U_{t}^{\top}}{n}.

The hidden blocks Σtu,Σtv\Sigma^{u}_{t},\Sigma^{v}_{t} do not enter the loss, but govern the predictor’s motion. We use the same notation Σ\Sigma whether the covariance is specified directly or realized by finite-width factors: the closed equation depends only on this matrix. Set GE:=(0E⊤E0)G_{E}:=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&E^{\top}\\ E&0\end{smallmatrix}\right), Gt:=GEtG_{t}:=G_{E_{t}}, and G⁡(S):=G∇ℓ​(S)G(S):=G_{\nabla\ell(S)}, so W˙t=−Gt​Wt\dot{W}_{t}=-G_{t}W_{t}. The split structure of the gradient is encoded by the signature matrix

J:=diag⁡(Iddu,−Iddv),Gt​J+J​Gt=0.J:=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}},-\mathrm{Id}_{d_{v}}),\qquad G_{t}J+JG_{t}=0.

Our first result combines covariance closure with width-independent spectral conservation laws.

Proposition 2.1 (Covariance closure and conservation laws).

Let ℋk​(Σ):=tr⁡((J​Σ)k)\mathcal{H}_{k}(\Sigma):=\operatorname{tr}\!\left((J\Sigma)^{k}\right). On its interval of existence, the factor flow (1) closes on the covariance Σt\Sigma_{t} as a Bures equation, for which the characteristic polynomial of J​ΣJ\Sigma is preserved:

Σ˙t=−(GtΣt+ΣtGt),dd​tℋk(Σt)=0,k=1,…,m,\dot{\Sigma}_{t}=-(G_{t}\Sigma_{t}+\Sigma_{t}G_{t}),\qquad\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{H}_{k}(\Sigma_{t})=0,\quad k=1,\ldots,m, (2)

The covariance equation (2) is the Bures gradient flow (Takatsu, 2011; Bhatia et al., 2019) of F⁡(Σ):=ℓ⁡(Σv​u)F(\Sigma):=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}), since ∇ΣF=G/2\nabla_{\Sigma}F=G/2. Its fundamental matrix Φt\Phi_{t}, defined by Φ˙t=−Gt​Φt\dot{\Phi}_{t}=-G_{t}\Phi_{t} and Φ0=Id\Phi_{0}=\mathrm{Id}, satisfies

Φt⊤​J​Φt=Φt​J​Φt⊤=J,Σt=Φt​Σ0​Φt⊤.\Phi_{t}^{\top}J\Phi_{t}=\Phi_{t}J\Phi_{t}^{\top}=J,\qquad\Sigma_{t}=\Phi_{t}\Sigma_{0}\Phi_{t}^{\top}. (3)

The functions ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} are conserved at every width nn, defining mean-field laws. Appendix B gives their measure formulation, the corresponding Wasserstein PDE, and describes a larger family of laws.

Conserved spectral margins

The spectral conservation laws (2) give uniform lower bounds on the spectrum of the hidden blocks (Σu,Σv)(\Sigma^{u},\Sigma^{v}) through two margins of the full covariance.

Definition 2.2 (Covariance support margins and gap).

For Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0, the support margins and their sum are

a±​(Σ):=max⁡{a≥0:Σ∓a​J⪰0},g⁡(Σ):=a+​(Σ)+a−​(Σ).a_{\pm}(\Sigma):=\max\{a\geq 0:\Sigma\mp aJ\succeq 0\},\qquad g(\Sigma):=a_{+}(\Sigma)+a_{-}(\Sigma). (4)

These maxima are finite and nonnegative. If λ1≤⋯≤λm\lambda_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{m} are the eigenvalues of Σ1/2​J​Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}J\Sigma^{1/2}, including zeros, then

a+​(Σ)=λdv+1,a−​(Σ)=−λdv,g⁡(Σ)=λdv+1−λdv.a_{+}(\Sigma)=\lambda_{d_{v}+1},\qquad a_{-}(\Sigma)=-\lambda_{d_{v}},\qquad g(\Sigma)=\lambda_{d_{v}+1}-\lambda_{d_{v}}. (5)

Thus g⁡(Σ)g(\Sigma) is an indexed spectral gap. Equivalently, it is the length of the positive-semidefinite interval [−a−​(Σ),a+​(Σ)][-a_{-}(\Sigma),a_{+}(\Sigma)] of the pencil Σ−t​J\Sigma-tJ; such intervals are standard in matrix-pencil theory (Nguyen and Nguyen, 2024). Appendix C proves (5), including at singular covariances. For Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0, a+​(Σ)a_{+}(\Sigma) and −a−​(Σ)-a_{-}(\Sigma) are the signed eigenvalues of Σ1/2​J​Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}J\Sigma^{1/2} nearest zero on their respective sides, and g⁡(Σ)≥2​λmin​(Σ)>0g(\Sigma)\geq 2\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)>0.

Proposition 2.3 (Transported lower bounds).

On its interval of existence, every solution of (2) from Σ0⪰0\Sigma_{0}\succeq 0 preserves a±​(Σt)=a±​(Σ0)a_{\pm}(\Sigma_{t})=a_{\pm}(\Sigma_{0}) and satisfies

Σt∓a±​(Σ0)​J⪰0,Σtu⪰a+​(Σ0)​Iddu,Σtv⪰a−​(Σ0)​Iddv.\Sigma_{t}\mp a_{\pm}(\Sigma_{0})J\succeq 0,\qquad\Sigma^{u}_{t}\succeq a_{+}(\Sigma_{0})\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}},\qquad\Sigma^{v}_{t}\succeq a_{-}(\Sigma_{0})\mathrm{Id}_{d_{v}}.

The margins a±​(Σ)a_{\pm}(\Sigma) need not equal the minimum eigenvalues of the initial hidden blocks: they satisfy a+​(Σ)≤λmin​(Σu)a_{+}(\Sigma)\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma^{u}) and a−​(Σ)≤λmin​(Σv)a_{-}(\Sigma)\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma^{v}), with equality when Σv​u=0\Sigma^{vu}=0. For instance, letting Σ=(1rr1)\Sigma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&r\\ r&1\end{smallmatrix}\right), |r|≤1|r|\leq 1, both margins are 1−r2\sqrt{1-r^{2}}, whereas both hidden variances are one. The support gap g⁡(Σ)g(\Sigma) controls predictor dissipation and can remain positive even when the full covariance is degenerate.

Under special conditions on the conserved spectrum of J​ΣJ\Sigma, elimination of hidden blocks becomes possible: Appendix E describes these intrinsic dynamics.

3 Linear convergence of training dynamics

Convergence of gradient flow

A positive conserved support gap g⁡(Σ0)>0g(\Sigma_{0})>0 guarantees global linear convergence for the Bures flow (2), including some cases where the initial covariance Σ0\Sigma_{0} is singular. Write Δt:=ℓ⁡(Σtv​u)−ℓ⋆\Delta_{t}:=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}_{t})-\ell_{\star} for the loss gap and 𝒮⋆\mathcal{S}_{\star} for the set of global predictor minimizers.

Theorem 3.1 (Global convergence from a positive support gap).

Under Assumption 1.1, let Σ0⪰0\Sigma_{0}\succeq 0 be a possibly singular covariance with g⁡(Σ0)>0g(\Sigma_{0})>0. Then the solution of (2) is global and satisfies

Δt≤Δ0​e−2​κ​g​(Σ0)​t,t≥0.\Delta_{t}\leq\Delta_{0}e^{-2\kappa g(\Sigma_{0})t},\qquad t\geq 0. (6)

As t→∞t\to\infty, Σt→Σ∞⪰0\Sigma_{t}\to\Sigma_{\infty}\succeq 0 with rank⁡Σ∞=rank⁡Σ0\operatorname{rank}\Sigma_{\infty}=\operatorname{rank}\Sigma_{0} and Σ∞v​u∈𝒮⋆\Sigma^{vu}_{\infty}\in\mathcal{S}_{\star}. The predictor Σv​u\Sigma^{vu} and any factor realization (as per (1)) converge linearly with rate κ​g​(Σ0)\kappa g(\Sigma_{0}) in Frobenius norm.

The only nondegeneracy requirement is g⁡(Σ0)>0g(\Sigma_{0})>0. Positive definiteness is sufficient but not necessary: Σ0≻0\Sigma_{0}\succ 0 implies g⁡(Σ0)≥2​λmin​(Σ0)>0g(\Sigma_{0})\geq 2\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{0})>0 and then Σ∞≻0\Sigma_{\infty}\succ 0. The exponent separates loss geometry (captured by the PL constant κ\kappa) from initial covariance conditioning (the support gap g⁡(Σ0)g(\Sigma_{0})), with no extra dimension factor. The trajectory selects a global minimizer according to its initialization and dynamics. Proposition C.4 supplies all explicit prefactors and bounds.

Remark 3.2 (Singular covariance and predictor rank).

The initialization Σ0=diag⁡(Iddu,0dv)\Sigma_{0}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}},0_{d_{v}}) has a+​(Σ0)=1a_{+}(\Sigma_{0})=1, a−​(Σ0)=0a_{-}(\Sigma_{0})=0, and g⁡(Σ0)=1g(\Sigma_{0})=1. Its rank is only dud_{u}, yet the theorem applies. There is no rank contradiction: a full-rank predictor needs rank min⁡(du,dv)\min(d_{u},d_{v}), not mm. More generally, a+​(Σ0)>0a_{+}(\Sigma_{0})>0 implies rank⁡Σ0≥du\operatorname{rank}\Sigma_{0}\geq d_{u}, while a−​(Σ0)>0a_{-}(\Sigma_{0})>0 implies rank⁡Σ0≥dv\operatorname{rank}\Sigma_{0}\geq d_{v}. The condition cannot be dropped altogether: for du=dv=2d_{u}=d_{v}=2, Σ0=diag⁡(1,0,1,0)\Sigma_{0}=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,1,0) and ℓ⁡(S):=‖S−e2​e2⊤‖F2/2\ell(S):=\left\lVert S-e_{2}e_{2}^{\top}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/2, the flow is stationary and nonoptimal. Here g⁡(Σ0)=0g(\Sigma_{0})=0, despite the nonzero signed eigenvalues +1,−1+1,-1.

Remark 3.3 (Quadratic specialization).

For ℓ⁡(S):=12​⟨𝒬⁡[S−Σ⋆v​u],S−Σ⋆v​u⟩\ell(S):=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\mathcal{Q}[S-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}],S-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}\right\rangle with 𝒬⪰0\mathcal{Q}\succeq 0 a nonzero self-adjoint linear operator, the exponent is 2​g​(Σ0)​λmin+​(𝒬)2g(\Sigma_{0})\lambda_{\min}^{+}(\mathcal{Q}). For a full-rank isotropic initialization Σ0=σ2​Idm\Sigma_{0}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}, one has a+​(Σ0)=a−​(Σ0)=σ2a_{+}(\Sigma_{0})=a_{-}(\Sigma_{0})=\sigma^{2}, giving a rate of 4​σ2​λmin+​(𝒬)4\sigma^{2}\lambda_{\min}^{+}(\mathcal{Q}). The operator 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is allowed to have a nontrivial kernel: the predictor Σv​u\Sigma^{vu} converges to a point in Σ⋆v​u+ker⁡𝒬\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}+\operatorname{ker}\mathcal{Q}. If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is positive definite, the predictor converges to the teacher Σ⋆v​u\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}.

For a quadratic predictor loss, Figure 2 compares the initialization scale, loss of conditioning, and the finite-width sampling we discuss next. The dotted curves use a coarse determinant-based rate, derived for comparison in Appendix C.3. If the support gap g⁡(Σ0)g(\Sigma_{0}) vanishes, trace and initial loss alone cannot guarantee a uniform positive rate (Example C.9). Figure 6 in Appendix F provides the counterpart for a non-quadratic smoothed-Lasso predictor loss.

We now focus on finite-width networks, whose initial empirical covariance is Σ0:=W0​W0⊤/n\Sigma_{0}:=W_{0}W_{0}^{\top}/n. For random initialization, the goal is to make this empirical covariance close to a prescribed population covariance Σ~0\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}, thereby retaining its support gap and convergence rate. Draw the columns wi:=(ui,vi)w_{i}:=(u_{i},v_{i}) of W0:=(U0V0)W_{0}:=\binom{U_{0}}{V_{0}} independently from the same subgaussian distribution: wi:=Σ~01/2​ξiw_{i}:=\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}\xi_{i}, where 𝔼⁡[ξi​ξi⊤]=Idm\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}]=\mathrm{Id}_{m} and sup‖z‖=1‖⟨z,ξi⟩‖ψ2≤K\sup_{\left\lVert z\right\rVert=1}\left\lVert\langle z,\xi_{i}\rangle\right\rVert_{\psi_{2}}\leq K. Remark 3.5 (Width and initialization geometry).

The condition g⁡(Σ~0)>0g(\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0})>0 forces r0≥min⁡(du,dv)r_{0}\geq\min(d_{u},d_{v}), and this minimum is attainable. If du≤dvd_{u}\leq d_{v}, take Σ~0=diag⁡(2​σ2​Iddu,0dv)\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}=\operatorname{diag}(2\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}},0_{d_{v}}), σ>0\sigma>0: then r0=dur_{0}=d_{u} and g⁡(Σ~0)=2​σ2g(\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0})=2\sigma^{2}. Convergence of gradient descent

Unlike finite-width sampling of neurons, discretized gradient descent in the factor matrices (U,V)(U,V) with a finite step size changes the covariance evolution itself. We show that sufficiently small step sizes retain global linear convergence by controlling the accumulated conservation error. We consider discrete-time gradient descent (GD) on the factor matrices, using an Euler discretization of (1) with step size τ\tau. As in the gradient flow setting, define Σk:=Wk​Wk⊤/n\Sigma_{k}:=W_{k}W_{k}^{\top}/n, Σkv​u:=Vk​Uk⊤/n\Sigma^{vu}_{k}:=V_{k}U_{k}^{\top}/n, and Δk:=ℓ⁡(Σkv​u)−ℓ⋆\Delta_{k}:=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}_{k})-\ell_{\star}. Setting Ek:=∇ℓ​(Σkv​u)E_{k}:=\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu}_{k}) and Gk:=GEkG_{k}:=G_{E_{k}}, the iterates read

Uk+1=Uk−τ​Ek⊤​Vk,Vk+1=Vk−τ​Ek​Uk.U_{k+1}=U_{k}-\tau E_{k}^{\top}V_{k},\qquad V_{k+1}=V_{k}-\tau E_{k}U_{k}. (8)

Equivalently, Wk+1=Wk−n​τ​∇Wℒ​(Uk,Vk)W_{k+1}=W_{k}-n\tau\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}(U_{k},V_{k}): this is GD for n​ℒn\mathcal{L} with stepsize τ\tau, or for ℒ\mathcal{L} with stepsize n​τn\tau. Writing Wk+1=Mk​WkW_{k+1}=M_{k}W_{k} with Mk:=Id−τ​GkM_{k}:=\mathrm{Id}-\tau G_{k} gives

Σk+1=Mk​Σk​Mk=Σk−τ⁡(Gk​Σk+Σk​Gk)+τ2​Gk​Σk​Gk.\Sigma_{k+1}=M_{k}\Sigma_{k}M_{k}=\Sigma_{k}-\tau(G_{k}\Sigma_{k}+\Sigma_{k}G_{k})+\tau^{2}G_{k}\Sigma_{k}G_{k}. (9)

The additional term τ2​Gk​Σk​Gk\tau^{2}G_{k}\Sigma_{k}G_{k} arises from taking the GD step in the individual factors (U,V)(U,V) and is absent from an Euler step taken directly on the Bures ODE.

A positive initial support gap g⁡(Σ0)g(\Sigma_{0}) still guarantees global linear convergence for sufficiently small step sizes τ\tau. The condition on τ\tau is given below and depends only on the initial covariance, initial loss gap, and loss parameters; it controls both descent and the accumulated conservation error.

Theorem 3.6 (Small-step global convergence of factor descent).

Under Assumption 1.1, let Σ0:=W0​W0⊤/n\Sigma_{0}:=W_{0}W_{0}^{\top}/n satisfy g⁡(Σ0)>0g(\Sigma_{0})>0, and suppose Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0. Set I⋆:=4​Δ0/κ/g⁡(Σ0)I_{\star}:=4\sqrt{\Delta_{0}/\kappa}/g(\Sigma_{0}). If

0<τ≤τGD:=g(Σ0)e−2​I⋆min{14​‖Σ0‖op​L​Δ0+9​2​L​‖Σ0‖op2​e2​I⋆,2−14​Δ0},0<\tau\leq\tau_{\rm GD}:=g(\Sigma_{0})e^{-2I_{\star}}\min\left\{\dfrac{1}{4\left\lVert\Sigma_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{L\Delta_{0}}+9\sqrt{2}L\left\lVert\Sigma_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}e^{2I_{\star}}},\quad\dfrac{\sqrt{2}-1}{4\Delta_{0}}\right\}, (10)

then, with q:=1−κ​τ​g​(Σ0)/2∈(0,1)q:=1-\kappa\tau g(\Sigma_{0})/\sqrt{2}\in(0,1) it holds that Δk≤qk​Δ0\Delta_{k}\leq q^{k}\Delta_{0}. Appendix C.5 gives the explicit expression for τGD\tau_{\rm GD} when Σ0=σ2​Idm\Sigma_{0}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m} and a comparison with the step-size condition obtained by linearizing near an equilibrium (Remark C.16). Corollary C.18 gives a step size chosen before sampling the factors, using the loss parameters and the bounds on the initial support gap, covariance norm, and loss gap from Theorem C.12.

4 Deep linear residual networks

We now turn to deep linear residual networks (ResNets), including a continuous-depth formulation. To stabilize optimization as depth increases, the networks considered here use skip connections between successive layers and scale each residual update by the inverse depth. In this section, we demonstrate that linear ResNets also enjoy global exponential convergence rates that remain uniform across depths, provided the average conserved layer support gap is bounded away from zero and the residual predictors satisfy an a priori operator-norm bound independent of depth throughout training. The latter is an additional hypothesis: layerwise conservation alone does not control forward and backward propagation. For simplicity, we state the results for gradient flow, as in Section 3.

Finite-depth setting

We consider a depth-SS, width-nn network with matching input and output dimensions du=dv=dd_{u}=d_{v}=d, and set h:=1/Sh:=1/S. For s=0,…,S−1s=0,\ldots,S-1, layer ss has factors Us,Vs∈ℝd×nU_{s},V_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}, covariance Σs:=Ws​Ws⊤/n\Sigma_{s}:=W_{s}W_{s}^{\top}/n with Ws:=(UsVs)W_{s}:=\binom{U_{s}}{V_{s}}, and predictor Σsv​u:=Vs​Us⊤/n\Sigma^{vu}_{s}:=V_{s}U_{s}^{\top}/n. xs+1=xs+1S​nVsUs⊤xs=Asxs,As:=Id+hΣv​us,s=0,…,S−1.x^{s+1}=x^{s}+\tfrac{1}{Sn}V_{s}U_{s}^{\top}x^{s}=A_{s}x^{s},\qquad A_{s}:=\mathrm{Id}+h\Sigma^{vu}_{s},\qquad s=0,\ldots,S-1.

Thus xS=PS​x0x^{S}=P_{S}x^{0}, where the endpoint predictor is the ordered product

For E:=∇ℓ​(PS)E:=\nabla\ell(P_{S}), the backpropagated gradient is E~s:=P>s⊤​E​P<s⊤\widetilde{E}_{s}:=P_{>s}^{\top}EP_{<s}^{\top}. In residual mean-field time, each layer obeys

Σ˙s=−(G~s​Σs+Σs​G~s),G~s:=GE~s.\dot{\Sigma}_{s}=-(\widetilde{G}_{s}\Sigma_{s}+\Sigma_{s}\widetilde{G}_{s}),\qquad\widetilde{G}_{s}:=G_{\widetilde{E}_{s}}. (11)

Under Assumption 1.1 for the endpoint loss, suppose Σs​(0)≻0\Sigma_{s}(0)\succ 0 for all ss, and write g¯S:=S−1​∑s=0S−1g⁡(Σs​(0))\overline{g}_{S}:=S^{-1}\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}g(\Sigma_{s}(0)) for the average initial support gap. Suppose sups‖Σsv​u​(t)‖op≤B<S\sup_{s}\left\lVert\Sigma^{vu}_{s}(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq B<S for some constant 0≤B<∞0\leq B<\infty on the maximal existence interval, and define the propagation lower bound σ¯S:=(1−B/S)S−1\underline{\sigma}_{S}:=(1-B/S)^{S-1}. Under Assumption 1.1 for the endpoint loss, consider a covariance profile satisfying the assumptions above, with Σs​(0)≻0\Sigma_{s}(0)\succ 0 for almost every ss. ℓ⁡(P⁡(t))−ℓ⋆≤(ℓ⁡(P⁡(0))−ℓ⋆)​e−2​κ​g¯​e−2​B​t.\ell(P(t))-\ell_{\star}\leq(\ell(P(0))-\ell_{\star})e^{-2\kappa\overline{g}e^{-2B}t}. (12)

As t→∞t\to\infty, Σs​(t)→Σs∞\Sigma_{s}(t)\to\Sigma_{s}^{\infty} for almost every depth ss, and profiles converge in L1​([0,1],𝕊2​d)L^{1}([0,1];\mathbb{S}^{2d}). The need for additional residual-path boundedness assumptions arises because the loss depends only on the endpoint s=1s=1: see Remark C.19 in Appendix C.6.

5 Heavy-ball momentum convergence

We now turn our attention to the analogous dynamics in an inertial setting that models heavy-ball momentum-based optimization. Upon introducing momentum, the system no longer closes on the position covariance of the neuron weights (u,v)(u,v) alone: one must instead consider the phase space of positions and velocities tracked jointly. We show that, in terms of the phase covariance, dynamics are again closed for linear networks. We derive conservation identities describing this phase geometry; energy dissipation and control of position deformation give the convergence certificate below.

Dynamics and phase closure

Inertia adds velocity as a state variable, so the natural moment over which the dynamics close is the joint position-velocity covariance. For W:=(UV)W:=\binom{U}{V}, predictor Σv​u:=V​U⊤/n\Sigma^{vu}:=VU^{\top}/n, and damping γ>0\gamma>0, write E:=∇ℓ​(Σv​u)E:=\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu}). The factor dynamics are

W¨+γ​W˙+G⁡(Σv​u)​W=0,G⁡(Σv​u):=(0E⊤E0).\ddot{W}+\gamma\dot{W}+G(\Sigma^{vu})W=0,\qquad G(\Sigma^{vu}):=\begin{pmatrix}0&E^{\top}\\ E&0\end{pmatrix}. (13)

Write (P,Q):=(U˙,V˙)(P,Q):=(\dot{U},\dot{V}), so the columns of WW and W˙\dot{W} are positions xi:=(ui,vi)x_{i}:=(u_{i},v_{i}) and velocities yi:=(pi,qi)y_{i}:=(p_{i},q_{i}) respectively. In this section Σ:=n−1​(WW˙)​(WW˙)⊤\Sigma:=n^{-1}\binom{W}{\dot{W}}\binom{W}{\dot{W}}^{\!\top} denotes the full 2​m2m-dimensional phase covariance. Its blocks are Σ(u,v):=W​W⊤/n\Sigma^{(u,v)}:=WW^{\top}/n, Σ(p,q):=W˙​W˙⊤/n\Sigma^{(p,q)}:=\dot{W}\dot{W}^{\top}/n, and Ξ:=W​W˙⊤/n\Xi:=W\dot{W}^{\top}/n; the predictor remains the v​uvu block of Σ(u,v)\Sigma^{(u,v)}. With Gt:=G⁡(Σtv​u)G_{t}:=G(\Sigma^{vu}_{t}), the closed equation is

Σ˙t=𝖬t​Σt+Σt​𝖬t⊤,Σt=(Σt(u,v)ΞtΞt⊤Σt(p,q)),𝖬t:=(0Idm−Gt−γ​Idm).\dot{\Sigma}_{t}=\mathsf{M}_{t}\Sigma_{t}+\Sigma_{t}\mathsf{M}_{t}^{\top},\qquad\Sigma_{t}=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{t}&\Xi_{t}\\ \Xi_{t}^{\top}&\Sigma^{(p,q)}_{t}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathsf{M}_{t}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathrm{Id}_{m}\\ -G_{t}&-\gamma\mathrm{Id}_{m}\end{pmatrix}. (14)

Appendix C.7 gives the particle equations, measure formulation, and blockwise expansion.

Conformal laws and mechanical energy

Without damping, the fundamental matrix generated by 𝖬t\mathsf{M}_{t} in (14) is symplectic; damping rescales the associated bilinear form exponentially in time.

Proposition 5.1 (Conformal phase conservation laws).

Let Jc:=(0Idm−Idm0)J_{\mathrm{c}}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathrm{Id}_{m}\\ -\mathrm{Id}_{m}&0\end{pmatrix}. The phase fundamental matrix Ψ˙t=𝖬t​Ψt\dot{\Psi}_{t}=\mathsf{M}_{t}\Psi_{t}, Ψ0=Id2​m\Psi_{0}=\mathrm{Id}_{2m} generated by 𝖬t\mathsf{M}_{t} satisfies

(Ψt)⊤​Jc​Ψt=e−γ​t​Jc,Σt=Ψt​Σ0​(Ψt)⊤.(\Psi_{t})^{\top}J_{\mathrm{c}}\Psi_{t}=e^{-\gamma t}J_{\mathrm{c}},\qquad\Sigma_{t}=\Psi_{t}\Sigma_{0}(\Psi_{t})^{\top}.

Consequently, the spectrum of eγ​t​Jc​Σte^{\gamma t}J_{\mathrm{c}}\Sigma_{t} and all its trace powers are constant. At the characteristic level, these identities imply that, for any two trajectories of the same flow, za:=(xa,ya)z_{a}:=(x_{a},y_{a}), zb:=(xb,yb)z_{b}:=(x_{b},y_{b}), eγ​t​za⊤​Jc​zbe^{\gamma t}z_{a}^{\top}J_{\mathrm{c}}z_{b} is conserved.

Special spectral values permit reduced phase dynamics, we describe these in Appendix E. As before, write Δt:=ℓ⁡(Σtv​u)−ℓ⋆\Delta_{t}:=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}_{t})-\ell_{\star} for the predictor loss gap. Define 𝒦t:=tr⁡(Σt(p,q))/2\mathcal{K}_{t}:=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{(p,q)}_{t})/2 and ℰt:=Δt+𝒦t\mathcal{E}_{t}:=\Delta_{t}+\mathcal{K}_{t} as the kinetic and mechanical excess energies. Differentiating ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} along (14) gives ℰ˙t=−2​γ​𝒦t\dot{\mathcal{E}}_{t}=-2\gamma\mathcal{K}_{t}. This identity gives global existence of the solution to (14) from every Σ0⪰0\Sigma_{0}\succeq 0 (Proposition C.22). The remaining task is to derive spectral lower bounds for Σt(u,v)\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{t}.

Global convergence

We seek an initialization condition on Σ0\Sigma_{0} that keeps Σt(u,v)\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{t} uniformly elliptic for the whole trajectory. Let a0:=λmin​(Σ0(u,v))>0a_{0}:=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{0})>0 and b0:=λmax​(Σ0(u,v))b_{0}:=\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{0}). λs​(γ):=as​κ​γρs+2​γ2,𝔖s​(γ):=4λs​(γ)​3​ℰ02​as.\lambda_{s}(\gamma):=\tfrac{a_{s}\kappa\gamma}{\rho_{s}+2\gamma^{2}},\qquad\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma):=\tfrac{4}{\lambda_{s}(\gamma)}\sqrt{\tfrac{3\mathcal{E}_{0}}{2a_{s}}}. (15)

Theorem 5.2 (Global linear rate from a phase-energy certificate).

Under Assumption 1.1, let Σ0⪰0\Sigma_{0}\succeq 0 with Σ0(u,v)≻0\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{0}\succ 0 and ℰ0>0\mathcal{E}_{0}>0. If 𝔖s​(γ)<s\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)<s for some s>0s>0, then for all t≥0t\geq 0,

as​Idm⪯Σt(u,v)⪯bs​Idm,ℰt≤3​ℰ0​e−λs​(γ)​t.a_{s}\mathrm{Id}_{m}\preceq\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{t}\preceq b_{s}\mathrm{Id}_{m},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{t}\leq 3\mathcal{E}_{0}e^{-\lambda_{s}(\gamma)t}.

The covariance Σt(u,v)\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{t} and any associated factors (Ut,Vt)(U_{t},V_{t}) evolving under (13) converge exponentially with rate λs/2\lambda_{s}/2 to limits with optimal predictor and Σ∞(u,v)≻0\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{\infty}\succ 0; Σt(p,q)\Sigma^{(p,q)}_{t} tends to zero.

Corollary 5.3 (Two-scale white initialization).

Under Assumption 1.1, let Σ0(u,v)=σv​u2​Idm\Sigma^{(u,v)}_{0}=\sigma_{vu}^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}, Ξ0=0\Xi_{0}=0, and Σ0(p,q)⪰0\Sigma^{(p,q)}_{0}\succeq 0 have trace m​σq​p2m\sigma_{qp}^{2}, with σv​u>0\sigma_{vu}>0, σq​p≥0\sigma_{qp}\geq 0. Then ℰ0=Δ+m​σq​p2/2\mathcal{E}_{0}=\Delta+m\sigma_{qp}^{2}/2, where Δ:=ℓ⁡(0)−ℓ⋆\Delta:=\ell(0)-\ell_{\star}. If ℰ0>0\mathcal{E}_{0}>0, the certificate is

2​γ2−s​κ​σv​u3​e−3​s4​3​ℰ0/2​γ+4​L​σv​u2​e2​s+2​2​L​ℰ0<0.2\gamma^{2}-\tfrac{s\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}e^{-3s}}{4\sqrt{3\mathcal{E}_{0}/2}}\gamma+4L\sigma_{vu}^{2}e^{2s}+2\sqrt{2L\mathcal{E}_{0}}<0.

Numerical view of the bootstrap certificate

Writing 𝔊s​(γ):=𝔖s​(γ)−s\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma):=\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)-s, Figure 3 shows the boundaries 𝔊s​(γ)=0\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma)=0 for 1≤σv​u≤1031\leq\sigma_{vu}\leq 10^{3}, with (du,dv)=(3,2)(d_{u},d_{v})=(3,2), κ=L=1\kappa=L=1, σq​p=1\sigma_{qp}=1, and ℓ⁡(0)−ℓ⋆=1\ell(0)-\ell_{\star}=1. The regions where 𝔊s​(γ)<0\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma)<0 specify the pairs (s,γ)(s,\gamma) for which Theorem 5.2 guarantees spectral bounds and exponential energy decay. For the two-scale initialization, sufficiently large σv​u\sigma_{vu} yields a nonempty interval of γ\gamma satisfying Corollary 5.3. For fixed initialization and damping, a smaller admissible ss gives a tighter tube and faster rate; Figure 5 illustrates the limiting rate at the feasibility boundary analyzed in Appendix C.10.

Figure 4 compares empirical losses with the upper bounds on ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} from Corollary C.29. Each upper bound curve uses an explicit, approximately optimal rate certified by Theorem 5.2 (see Proposition C.28); no rate is fitted to the empirical trajectory. All displayed losses stay below their upper bounds. Notably in this inertial setting, the predictor loss may oscillate even while the mechanical energy decreases.

6 Conclusion

The present work addresses two-layer linear networks, making use of the exact closure of mean-field training on the neuron law covariance as a finite-dimensional Bures flow. This flow enjoys conservation laws that control the ellipticity of the predictor preconditioner through a conserved spectral support gap, yielding global linear convergence whenever this gap is positive. In particular, this is guaranteed for every positive-definite initial covariance and for smooth PL predictor losses. We show that this guarantee survives finite-width sampling of neurons, and extends to discrete-time gradient descent in the factors through approximate versions of the same conservation laws. The covariance viewpoint clarifies two further extensions: for deep linear ResNets, the same conservation law holds layerwise and gives linear convergence conditional on bounded residual paths. Heavy-ball momentum dynamics close in the joint phase covariance, where conformal conservation laws and mechanical energy lead to an explicit damping certificate from general initial phase moments. The certificate includes two-scale white initializations without imposing a phase-covariance identity. Covariance conditioning is the common quantitative mechanism throughout our analysis.

Appendix B Measure formulation and Wasserstein conservation laws

The covariance equations in the main text have the same meaning at both finite and infinite widths. In this section, we introduce the measure flow that captures training dynamics, define a law shared by all widths, and lift the spectral invariants to functionals of a neuron distribution.

B.1 Neuron distributions and Wasserstein flow

We describe the configuration of any number of neurons by their law: for w:=(u,v)∈ℝmw:=(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, let μ∈𝒫2​(ℝm)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{m}) and write its uncentered second moment

Σ⁡(μ):=∫w​w⊤​𝑑μ​(w).\Sigma(\mu):=\int ww^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}\mu(w). (16)

For nn neurons W:=(w1,…,wn)W:=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}), the neuron law is an empirical distribution μ^W:=n−1​∑i=1nδwi\widehat{\mu}_{W}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{w_{i}}, for which Σ⁡(μ^W)=W​W⊤/n\Sigma(\widehat{\mu}_{W})=WW^{\top}/n. A general covariance Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0 is also realized by a centered Gaussian distribution. The loss functional is ℱ⁡(μ):=ℓ⁡(Σv​u​(μ))\mathcal{F}(\mu):=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}(\mu)), so ℱ⁡(μ^W)=ℒ⁡(U,V)\mathcal{F}(\widehat{\mu}_{W})=\mathcal{L}(U,V).

For a functional with a sufficiently regular first variation, the Wasserstein gradient is the spatial gradient ∇W2ℱ​(μ)​(w):=∇w(δ​ℱ/δ​μ)​(μ,w)\nabla_{W_{2}}\mathcal{F}(\mu)(w):=\nabla_{w}(\delta\mathcal{F}/\delta\mu)(\mu,w) and its negative is the velocity in the continuity equation

∂tμt+∇w⋅(μt​bt)=0,bt:=−∇W2ℱ​(μt).\partial_{t}\mu_{t}+\nabla_{w}\cdot(\mu_{t}b_{t})=0,\qquad b_{t}:=-\nabla_{W_{2}}\mathcal{F}(\mu_{t}). (17)

The PDE is understood distributionally, including for empirical measures. In the present split model, δ​ℱ/δ​μ=12​w⊤​Gt​w\delta\mathcal{F}/\delta\mu=\tfrac{1}{2}w^{\top}G_{t}w up to an additive constant. Consequently,

∂tμt=∇w⋅(μt​Gt​w),μt=(Φt)#​μ0,\partial_{t}\mu_{t}=\nabla_{w}\cdot(\mu_{t}G_{t}w),\qquad\mu_{t}=(\Phi_{t})_{\#}\mu_{0}, (18)

where Φt\Phi_{t} is the fundamental matrix in (3). For the empirical neuron law, the characteristics of (17) are exactly u˙i=−Et⊤​vi\dot{u}_{i}=-E_{t}^{\top}v_{i}, v˙i=−Et​ui\dot{v}_{i}=-E_{t}u_{i}.

Conversely, given a solution Σt\Sigma_{t} of (2), transporting any initial distribution with second moment Σ0\Sigma_{0} by Φ˙t=−Gt​Φt\dot{\Phi}_{t}=-G_{t}\Phi_{t} produces a Wasserstein gradient flow with second moment Σt\Sigma_{t}. Indeed, its second moment and Σt\Sigma_{t} solve the same linear equation with the same initial data. Matching covariances alone does not ensure that a measure curve follows this gradient flow.

B.2 Covariance-dependent objectives

Moment closure is not specific to the off-diagonal predictor: the gradient flow of any sufficiently regular objective depending on second moments closes in terms of a Bures equation.

Proposition B.1 (Second-moment closure).

Let FF be a differentiable scalar function on an open neighborhood of 𝕊+m\mathbb{S}_{+}^{m} in the symmetric matrices, and define ℱ⁡(μ):=F⁡(Σ⁡(μ))\mathcal{F}(\mu):=F(\Sigma(\mu)). Let μt\mu_{t} be a sufficiently regular Wasserstein gradient flow of ℱ\mathcal{F}, and set Σt:=Σ⁡(μt)\Sigma_{t}:=\Sigma(\mu_{t}) and Dt:=∇ΣF​(Σt)D_{t}:=\nabla_{\Sigma}F(\Sigma_{t}). Then the characteristics satisfy w˙t=−2​Dt​wt\dot{w}_{t}=-2D_{t}w_{t}, and the second moment evolves autonomously as Σ˙t=−2​(Dt​Σt+Σt​Dt)\dot{\Sigma}_{t}=-2(D_{t}\Sigma_{t}+\Sigma_{t}D_{t}). Thus the Wasserstein flow of ℱ\mathcal{F} closes exactly on the Bures gradient flow of FF on second moments, with the normalization used throughout the paper.

Proof of Proposition B.1.

The first variation of ℱ\mathcal{F} at μt\mu_{t}, up to an additive constant, is δ​ℱδ​μ​(μt,w)=⟨Dt,w​w⊤⟩=w⊤​Dt​w\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t},w)=\left\langle D_{t},ww^{\top}\right\rangle=w^{\top}D_{t}w. Taking its Euclidean gradient in ww gives 2​Dt​w2D_{t}w and hence the claimed characteristic equation. Finally, writing the flow map as w0↦wtw_{0}\mapsto w_{t} and differentiating Σt=∫wt​wt⊤​d​μ0​(w0)\Sigma_{t}=\int w_{t}w_{t}^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(w_{0}) gives

Σ˙t=∫(w˙t​wt⊤+wt​w˙t⊤)​d​μ0​(w0)=−2​(Dt​Σt+Σt​Dt).∎\dot{\Sigma}_{t}=\int\left(\dot{w}_{t}w_{t}^{\top}+w_{t}\dot{w}_{t}^{\top}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(w_{0})=-2(D_{t}\Sigma_{t}+\Sigma_{t}D_{t}).\qed

B.3 Width consistency and covariance-level laws

We seek conservation laws defined on neuron distributions that remain conserved when evaluated on finite networks of any width.

Definition B.2 (Mean-field conservation law).

A scalar functional ℋ⁡(μ)\mathcal{H}(\mu) is a mean-field conservation law for a family of flows if it is constant along every admissible trajectory of every flow in that family, for every admissible initialization. It is covariance-level if ℋ⁡(μ)=h⁡(Σ⁡(μ))\mathcal{H}(\mu)=h(\Sigma(\mu)).

For differentiable functionals, the chain rule expresses conservation as orthogonality:

dd​tℋ(μt)=−∫∇W2ℋ(μt)⋅∇W2ℱ(μt)dμt=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{H}(\mu_{t})=-\int\nabla_{W_{2}}\mathcal{H}(\mu_{t})\cdot\nabla_{W_{2}}\mathcal{F}(\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}=0,

whenever taking gradients and the chain rule are well-defined. The laws below also have a direct characteristic proof. A single mean-field law ℋ\mathcal{H} induces laws hn​(W):=ℋ⁡(μ^W)h_{n}(W):=\mathcal{H}(\widehat{\mu}_{W}) for every width, in the finite-dimensional sense of Marcotte et al. (2023). Unrelated laws found separately at each width need not arise this way. Conversely, conservation at every finite width passes to the measure flow whenever the empirical flows converge in W2W_{2} and ℋ\mathcal{H} is continuous in that metric. For covariance-level laws no limiting argument is needed: every positive semidefinite covariance has an empirical realization, and the common closed moment equation gives the equivalence with Bures laws.

B.4 Gram-function laws and their spectral restriction

Preservation of pairwise indefinite products yields functionals that need not depend only on covariance.

Proposition B.3 (Fundamental mean-field laws).

Let μt=(Φt)#​μ0\mu_{t}=(\Phi_{t})_{\#}\mu_{0} be the characteristic flow of w˙t=−Gt​wt\dot{w}_{t}=-G_{t}w_{t}, where Gt⊤=GtG_{t}^{\top}=G_{t} and Gt​J+J​Gt=0G_{t}J+JG_{t}=0. For every r≥1r\geq 1 and Borel function φ:𝕊r→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{S}^{r}\to\mathbb{R}, the functional

In particular, the spectral laws ℋk​(Σ​(μ))\mathcal{H}_{k}(\Sigma(\mu)) of (2) are conserved for every μ0∈𝒫2​(ℝm)\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{m}). ℋk(Σt)=tr((−Γt/n)k),k≥1.\mathcal{H}_{k}(\Sigma_{t})=\operatorname{tr}\!\left((-\Gamma_{t}/n)^{k}\right),\qquad k\geq 1. (20)

The nonzero spectra of J​ΣtJ\Sigma_{t} and −Γt/n-\Gamma_{t}/n coincide.

Proof of Proposition B.3.

Along characteristics, dd​t​(wa⊤​J​wb)=−wa⊤​(Gt​J+J​Gt)​wb=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(w_{a}^{\top}Jw_{b})=-w_{a}^{\top}(G_{t}J+JG_{t})w_{b}=0, so (19) is conserved. Appendix C Technical details and proofs

C.1 Loss estimates

Lemma C.1 (Smooth PL consequences).

Under Assumption 1.1, the minimizer set 𝒮⋆:={S:ℓ⁡(S)=ℓ⋆}\mathcal{S}_{\star}:=\{S:\ell(S)=\ell_{\star}\} is nonempty, and

‖∇ℓ​(S)‖F2≤2​L​(ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆),dist⁡(S,𝒮⋆)2≤2​(ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆)/κ.\left\lVert\nabla\ell(S)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\leq 2L(\ell(S)-\ell_{\star}),\qquad\operatorname{dist}(S,\mathcal{S}_{\star})^{2}\leq 2(\ell(S)-\ell_{\star})/\kappa. (21)

For every perturbation HH,

ℓ⁡(S+H)−ℓ⋆≤ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆+L/2​‖H‖F.\sqrt{\ell(S+H)-\ell_{\star}}\leq\sqrt{\ell(S)-\ell_{\star}}+\sqrt{L/2}\left\lVert H\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}. (22)
Proof of Lemma C.1.

Apply the descent lemma at S−∇ℓ​(S)/LS-\nabla\ell(S)/L for the first inequality. Since ∇ℓ\nabla\ell is globally Lipschitz, the Euclidean gradient flow S˙=−∇ℓ​(S)\dot{S}=-\nabla\ell(S) exists for all t≥0t\geq 0. Writing h:=ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆h:=\ell(S)-\ell_{\star} gives h˙=−‖∇ℓ‖2\dot{h}=-\left\lVert\nabla\ell\right\rVert^{2} and, where h>0h>0, −dd​t​h≥κ/2​‖S˙‖-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sqrt{h}\geq\sqrt{\kappa/2}\left\lVert\dot{S}\right\rVert. Thus its total remaining length is at most 2​h/κ\sqrt{2h/\kappa}. The flow has a limit, with loss gap zero by PL, proving attainment and the distance bound. Finally, the descent lemma and the first inequality bound the perturbed loss gap by (h+L/2​‖H‖F)2(\sqrt{h}+\sqrt{L/2}\left\lVert H\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}})^{2}. ∎

Remark C.2 (Quadratic growth and convexity).

Lemma C.1 proves the quadratic-growth bound

ℓ⁡(S)−ℓ⋆≥λ2​dist⁡(S,𝒮⋆)2with ​λ=κ.\ell(S)-\ell_{\star}\geq\frac{\lambda}{2}\operatorname{dist}(S,\mathcal{S}_{\star})^{2}\qquad\text{with }\lambda=\kappa. (23)

If a larger quadratic-growth constant λ\lambda is known, it improves the distance bounds while leaving the loss rates, which use κ\kappa, unchanged. The PL-to-quadratic-growth implication does not need convexity (Karimi et al., 2016). Conversely, convex quadratic growth with constant λ\lambda implies PL with constant λ/4\lambda/4: for a nearest minimizer S⋆S_{\star}, Δ≤⟨∇ℓ​(S),S−S⋆⟩≤‖∇ℓ​(S)‖F​2​Δ/λ\Delta\leq\left\langle\nabla\ell(S),S-S_{\star}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert\nabla\ell(S)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\sqrt{2\Delta/\lambda}. The best PL and quadratic-growth constants need not coincide. For a nonzero quadratic Hessian 𝒬⪰0\mathcal{Q}\succeq 0, λ=κ=λmin+​(𝒬)\lambda=\kappa=\lambda_{\min}^{+}(\mathcal{Q}) is valid and 𝒮⋆=Σ⋆v​u+ker⁡𝒬\mathcal{S}_{\star}=\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}+\operatorname{ker}\mathcal{Q}.

C.2 Covariance closure and conservation laws

Direct matrix differentiation proves closure and conservation at every width. The measure interpretation is given separately in Appendix B.

Proof of Proposition 2.1.

Since W˙t=−Gt​Wt\dot{W}_{t}=-G_{t}W_{t} and Gt⊤=GtG_{t}^{\top}=G_{t}, differentiating Wt​Wt⊤/nW_{t}W_{t}^{\top}/n gives (2). For any covariance solution, define Φ˙t=−Gt​Φt\dot{\Phi}_{t}=-G_{t}\Phi_{t}, Φ0=Id\Phi_{0}=\mathrm{Id}. The same argument can use any independently established hidden-block lower bounds. The common-bound formulation below uses 2​c2c in place of g⁡(Σ0)g(\Sigma_{0}). Lemma C.5 (Conditional hidden-block criterion).

Under Assumption 1.1, start (2) from Σ0≻0\Sigma_{0}\succ 0. If Σtu⪰c​Id\Sigma^{u}_{t}\succeq c\mathrm{Id} and Σtv⪰c​Id\Sigma^{v}_{t}\succeq c\mathrm{Id} for some c>0c>0 throughout its maximal existence interval, the flow is global and

Δt≤Δ0​e−4​κ​c​t.\Delta_{t}\leq\Delta_{0}e^{-4\kappa ct}. (31)

Moreover Σt\Sigma_{t} converges to Σ∞≻0\Sigma_{\infty}\succ 0 with Σ∞v​u∈𝒮⋆\Sigma^{vu}_{\infty}\in\mathcal{S}_{\star}.

Quadratic growth further gives dist⁡(Σtv​u,𝒮⋆)2≤2​Δ0​e−4​κ​c​t/λ\operatorname{dist}(\Sigma^{vu}_{t},\mathcal{S}_{\star})^{2}\leq 2\Delta_{0}e^{-4\kappa ct}/\lambda, where λ=κ\lambda=\kappa is always available.

Proof of Lemma C.5.

The assumed hidden bounds give −Δ˙≥2​c​‖E‖F2≥4​c​κ​Δ-\dot{\Delta}\geq 2c\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\geq 4c\kappa\Delta. On every positive loss gap interval, differentiating Δt\sqrt{\Delta_{t}} gives

‖Σt‖op≤‖Σ0‖op​exp⁡(1c​2​Δ0κ),λmin​(Σt)≥λmin​(Σ0)​exp⁡(−1c​2​Δ0κ).\left\lVert\Sigma_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\left\lVert\Sigma_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta_{0}}{\kappa}}\right),\qquad\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{t})\geq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{0})\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta_{0}}{\kappa}}\right). These bounds rule out finite-time blow-up. The tail of the integral proves convergence to a positive-definite covariance with optimal predictor. Quadratic growth gives the distance bound. ∎

For coercive losses, determinant conservation and the second spectral law yield an alternative, generally much coarser, source of such bounds.

ccoarse:=α​(αm​α2+2​M2+M)m−1.c_{\rm coarse}:=\alpha\left(\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{m\alpha^{2}+2M^{2}}+M}\right)^{m-1}.

In the 2×22\times 2 covariance setting of Section 2, write Σ=(prrq)\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}p&r\\ r&q\end{pmatrix}, b0:=(p0−q0)/2b_{0}:=(p_{0}-q_{0})/2, and α2:=p0​q0−r02\alpha^{2}:=p_{0}q_{0}-r_{0}^{2}, with predictor loss ℓ⁡(r):=(r−β)2/2\ell(r):=(r-\beta)^{2}/2. For example, when β=1\beta=1 and p0=q0=1p_{0}=q_{0}=1, r0=−1r_{0}=-1, one has pt=qt=−rt=(2​e2​t−1)−1p_{t}=q_{t}=-r_{t}=(2e^{2t}-1)^{-1}. When β=0\beta=0, one has rt=r0/(1+2​|r0|​t)r_{t}=r_{0}/(1+2|r_{0}|t): convergence to the optimal apex is algebraic for r0≠0r_{0}\neq 0. Proof of Corollary 3.4.

The rank improvement in Remark 3.5 concerns the chosen population law. A positive population support gap alone does not guarantee a positive empirical support gap at small width when Σ~0=σ2​Idm\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}, σ>0\sigma>0.

Example C.11 (Isotropic Gaussian sampling can lose the support gap).

Let du=Dd_{u}=D, dv=1d_{v}=1, and sample from N⁡(0,Σ~0)N(0,\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}) with Σ~0=σ2​IdD+1\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{D+1}, σ>0\sigma>0. For independent ui∼N⁡(0,σ2​Iddu)u_{i}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}}) and vi∼N⁡(0,σ2​Iddv)v_{i}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{v}}), and the quadratic loss ℓ⁡(S):=‖S−Σ⋆v​u‖F2/2\ell(S):=\left\lVert S-\Sigma^{vu}_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/2, one has exactly

Remark C.16 (Local stability and the global stepsize).

Suppose ℓ\ell is C2C^{2} near a minimizer at zero, and linearize at Σ=σ2​Id\Sigma=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}. The predictor perturbation evolves to first order by δ​Σv​u↦(Id−2​τ​σ2​∇2ℓ​(0))​[δ​Σv​u]\delta\Sigma^{vu}\mapsto(\mathrm{Id}-2\tau\sigma^{2}\nabla^{2}\ell(0))[\delta\Sigma^{vu}]. Proof of Corollary C.18.

On (38), the empirical descent scale is at least α¯⋆\overline{\alpha}_{\star}, whereas the empirical loss gap, force bound, length bound, and covariance upper bound are at most their barred counterparts. If the realized initial loss gap vanishes, the empirical factors are stationary, and the conclusions hold directly. ∎

Boundary cases

For the scalar loss ℓ⁡(s):=(s+1)2/2\ell(s):=(s+1)^{2}/2, the singular initialization U0=V0≠0U_{0}=V_{0}\neq 0 preserves equality of the factors and keeps Σkv​u=‖Uk‖2/n≥0\Sigma^{vu}_{k}=\left\lVert U_{k}\right\rVert^{2}/n\geq 0, so its loss gap is at least 1/21/2. Conversely, even full-rank isotropic initialization does not justify arbitrary steps: for ℓ⁡(s):=(s−1)2/2\ell(s):=(s-1)^{2}/2, Σ0=Id2\Sigma_{0}=\mathrm{Id}_{2}, and τ=1\tau=1, one gets Σ1=(2222)\Sigma_{1}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\ 2&2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) and Σ2=0\Sigma_{2}=0, after which training is trapped.

Remark C.19 (Sharpness of the boundedness hypothesis).

Unlike the two-layer flow of Theorem 3.1, positive conserved layer margins do not rule out unbounded weight growth as S→∞S\to\infty or along continuous-depth training. A linear neural ODE has positive determinant, so it cannot fit an orientation-reversing target; training may instead approach a singular endpoint through unbounded residuals. For a concrete example, take the invertible scalar target p⋆:=−1p_{\star}:=-1 and loss ℓ⁡(p):=(p+1)2/2\ell(p):=(p+1)^{2}/2, with L=κ=1L=\kappa=1. Initialize every layer with Σs​(0)=Id2\Sigma_{s}(0)=\mathrm{Id}_{2}, realizable at width n=2n=2; every conserved support gap equals 22. At each finite depth S≥2S\geq 2, all residuals decrease to −S-S, so supt≥0maxs⁡|Σsv​u​(t)|=S\sup_{t\geq 0}\max_{s}|\Sigma^{vu}_{s}(t)|=S and no uniform B<SB<S exists. In continuous depth they decrease without bound, giving supt≥0∫01|Σsv​u​(t)|​𝑑s=∞\sup_{t\geq 0}\int_{0}^{1}|\Sigma^{vu}_{s}(t)|\,\mathrm{d}s=\infty. Both flows are global, but their endpoints tend to zero and their losses to 1/2>ℓ⋆=01/2>\ell_{\star}=0. At finite depth the target is representable: failure occurs along this symmetric trajectory, whereas the neural ODE excludes the target altogether. In both cases, positive conserved margins therefore fail to ensure the residual bounds required by the theorems.

Remark C.20 (Zero-target variant).

The same path bounds can fail while the loss tends to zero. Remark C.21 (Residual-path control and orientation).

Positive-definite layer covariances can coexist with singular residual products. For a scalar depth-two network, take both layer predictors equal to −2-2, so A0=A1=0A_{0}=A_{1}=0, and the endpoint loss ℓ⁡(p):=(p−1)2/2\ell(p):=(p-1)^{2}/2. Both backpropagated gradients vanish although the endpoint is not optimal. These predictors admit positive-definite layer covariances (5−2−25)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sqrt{5}&-2\\ -2&\sqrt{5}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr), whose signed eigenvalues are +1,−1+1,-1. Extending the earlier discretization and sampling arguments to this setting requires control of the residual products along the corresponding training trajectory; the two-layer GD theorem does not apply verbatim.

In continuous depth, detP⁡(t)=exp⁡(∫01tr⁡Σsv​u​(t)​𝑑s)>0\det P(t)=\exp(\int_{0}^{1}\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^{vu}_{s}(t)\,\mathrm{d}s)>0. The uniform path bound also keeps σmin​(P⁡(t))≥e−B\sigma_{\min}(P(t))\geq e^{-B}, so any convergent endpoint remains in the orientation-preserving invertible component. If every global minimizer has negative determinant, these path bounds are incompatible with convergence to a global minimizer.

C.8 An exact decomposition of hidden kinetic energy

Prescribing the position covariance and its derivative does not determine the kinetic energy: velocity components that leave the covariance unchanged can still contribute to it.

Proposition C.25 (Minimum-energy lift of a covariance velocity).

Fix A≻0A\succ 0 and a symmetric matrix HH as the desired value of A˙\dot{A}. Let C=C⊤C=C^{\top} be the unique solution of C​A+A​C=HCA+AC=H. Every positive semidefinite phase covariance with this position moment and derivative has regression coordinates

D=C+Ω,Ω​A+A​Ω⊤=0,Q⪰0,D=C+\Omega,\qquad\Omega A+A\Omega^{\top}=0,\qquad Q\succeq 0,

and its kinetic energy decomposes as

𝒦=12​tr⁡(C​A​C)+12​tr⁡(Ω​A​Ω⊤)+12​tr⁡Q.\mathcal{K}=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(CAC)+\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Omega A\Omega^{\top})+\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}Q. (62)

Thus the graph lift D=CD=C, Q=0Q=0 has minimum kinetic energy. An additional positive semidefinite Schur complement contributes exactly tr⁡Q/2\operatorname{tr}Q/2.

Proof.

In an eigenbasis of AA, the Sylvester equation divides Hi​jH_{ij} by the strictly positive sum of eigenvalues, proving existence and uniqueness. Equation D​A+A​D⊤=HDA+AD^{\top}=H is equivalent to the stated condition on Ω\Omega. Since B=D​A​D⊤+QB=DAD^{\top}+Q, expand its trace. The two cross terms vanish in sum: Ω​A\Omega A is skew-symmetric and CC is symmetric. Each term in (62) is nonnegative. ∎

Example C.26 (Identical position covariance and covariance derivative, arbitrarily large energy).

Let A=σ2​IdmA=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}, C=0C=0, choose any skew-symmetric Ω\Omega, and set D=ΩD=\Omega, Q=0Q=0. The initial predictor is zero because A=σ2​IdmA=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}, and A˙=0\dot{A}=0 makes its derivative zero as well, independently of Ω\Omega. Nevertheless 𝒦=σ2​‖Ω‖F2/2\mathcal{K}=\sigma^{2}\left\lVert\Omega\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/2 can be arbitrarily large. The phase covariance is positive semidefinite; nonzero Ω\Omega gives a nonsymmetric regression matrix. For fixed a0,b0,L,κa_{0},b_{0},L,\kappa, the best feasibility ratio (84) tends to zero as ℰ0→∞\mathcal{E}_{0}\to\infty. Thus the initial position covariance and predictor speed do not determine whether the energy-damping certificate holds.

The role of the prefactor

A faster conditional exponent must be accompanied by its own prefactor when testing the global deformation budget. The sharper state-dependent prefactor uses the initial loss derivative Δ˙0=⟨E0,Σ0q​u+Σ0v​p⟩\dot{\Delta}_{0}=\langle E_{0},\Sigma^{qu}_{0}+\Sigma^{vp}_{0}\rangle as well as total energy. In particular, zero predictor speed gives ℭ0=1/(1−q)\mathfrak{C}_{0}=1/(1-q). The parameter-only prefactor uses no extra initial derivative. Maximizing the conditional exponent alone need not minimize the global budget: the same choice of parameters also changes qq and hence the prefactor. The closed-form optimizer should therefore be tested in (81), not substituted there with an unchanged prefactor.

C.10 Large-position-scale certificate asymptotics

Increasing position variance can open a damping window without reducing the initial loss gap. We quantify that tradeoff and the best rates certified by the same bootstrap. For the two-scale white initialization of Corollary 5.3, the initial mechanical excess energy is

ℰ0=ℓ⁡(0)−ℓ⋆+m​σq​p22.\mathcal{E}_{0}=\ell(0)-\ell_{\star}+\frac{m\sigma_{qp}^{2}}{2}.

This quantity is fixed when σq​p\sigma_{qp} is fixed and σv​u→+∞\sigma_{vu}\to+\infty. It is useful to name the bootstrap gap

𝔊s​(γ):=𝔖s​(γ)−s,scert​(γ):=inf{s>0:𝔊s​(γ)<0}.\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma):=\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)-s,\qquad s_{\mathrm{cert}}(\gamma):=\inf\{s>0:\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma)<0\}.

Whenever this set is nonempty, define the corresponding boundary rate by

λcert​(γ):=λscert​(γ)​(γ),\lambda_{\mathrm{cert}}(\gamma):=\lambda_{s_{\mathrm{cert}}(\gamma)}(\gamma),

using continuity in ss. The strict bootstrap condition need not hold at the boundary itself: the theorem applies at interior budgets s>scerts>s_{\mathrm{cert}} with 𝔊s​(γ)<0\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma)<0, whose rates approach this boundary value. Thus λcert\lambda_{\mathrm{cert}} is a limiting supremal certificate, rather than a rate asserted at a possibly nonadmissible boundary point. Define also the largest damping for which the bootstrap window is nonempty:

γmaxcert​(σv​u):=sup{γ>0: there exists ​s>0​ such that ​𝔊s​(γ)<0}.\gamma^{\mathrm{cert}}_{\max}(\sigma_{vu}):=\sup\{\gamma>0:\text{ there exists }s>0\text{ such that }\mathfrak{G}_{s}(\gamma)<0\}.

The assumption ℰ0>0\mathcal{E}_{0}>0 below excludes only the trivial zero-excess case, in which both the predictor loss gap and kinetic energy vanish and the trajectory is stationary.

At a fixed deformation budget, admissibility reduces to a quadratic inequality, making both damping boundaries explicit. For ℰ0>0\mathcal{E}_{0}>0 and fixed deformation budget s>0s>0, write

cs:=s​κ​as3/24​3​ℰ0/2.c_{s}:=\frac{s\kappa a_{s}^{3/2}}{4\sqrt{3\mathcal{E}_{0}/2}}. (82)

cs2>8​ρs,cs−cs2−8​ρs4<γ<cs+cs2−8​ρs4.c_{s}^{2}>8\rho_{s},\qquad\frac{c_{s}-\sqrt{c_{s}^{2}-8\rho_{s}}}{4}<\gamma<\frac{c_{s}+\sqrt{c_{s}^{2}-8\rho_{s}}}{4}. (83)

𝔖s​(γ)≥8​γ​e3​sκ​σv​u3​3​ℰ02,\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)\geq\frac{8\gamma e^{3s}}{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}}\sqrt{\frac{3\mathcal{E}_{0}}{2}},

and hence

γ<κ​σv​u38​3​ℰ0/2​s​e−3​s≤κ​σv​u324​e​3​ℰ0/2.\gamma<\frac{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}}{8\sqrt{3\mathcal{E}_{0}/2}}\,se^{-3s}\leq\frac{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}}{24e\sqrt{3\mathcal{E}_{0}/2}}.

This proves the required asymptotic upper bound uniformly over all budgets, not only over bounded ss.

For the matching lower bound, take γ\gamma of order σv​u3\sigma_{vu}^{3} and keep ss in a compact subset of (0,+∞)(0,+\infty). Then 2​γ22\gamma^{2} dominates ρs\rho_{s} in (15), and

λs​(γ)=κ​σv​u2​e−2​s2​γ​(1+o⁡(1)).\lambda_{s}(\gamma)=\frac{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{2}e^{-2s}}{2\gamma}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr).

Consequently,

𝔖s​(γ)=8​γ​e3​sκ​σv​u3​3​ℰ02​(1+o⁡(1)),\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)=\frac{8\gamma e^{3s}}{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}}\sqrt{\frac{3\mathcal{E}_{0}}{2}}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),

so the condition 𝔖s​(γ)<s\mathfrak{S}_{s}(\gamma)<s is asymptotically equivalent to

γ<κ​σv​u38​3​ℰ0/2​s​e−3​s.\gamma<\frac{\kappa\sigma_{vu}^{3}}{8\sqrt{3\mathcal{E}_{0}/2}}\,se^{-3s}.

The right-hand side is maximized at s=1/3s=1/3. Choosing this budget and any fixed multiplicative factor below the maximum gives an admissible pair for all sufficiently large σv​u\sigma_{vu}, proving the matching lower bound and the claimed asymptotic formula. ∎

Proposition C.31 has two complementary messages. At fixed damping, increasing the initial position scale makes the certified ellipticity deformation vanish and the certified rate converges to κ​γ/(4​L)\kappa\gamma/(4L). At fixed σv​u\sigma_{vu}, however, this particular bootstrap theorem cannot certify arbitrarily large damping: the admissible region in (s,γ)(s,\gamma) eventually disappears, with the upper edge scaling like σv​u3\sigma_{vu}^{3}. This is a limitation of the certificate, not a claim that the underlying damped dynamics fail in the large-damping regime.

Appendix D Counting covariance-level mean-field laws

This appendix records the Lie-algebra computation behind the covariance-level completeness statement used in Section 2. It is a continuum, covariance-level analogue of the local/generic finite-width completeness theorem of Marcotte et al. (2023).

Width-consistent laws and their Wasserstein interpretation are defined in Appendix B. We work here directly with functions of the covariance and the vector fields that must annihilate them.

D.1 Split Bures vector fields

To characterize the laws shared by the architecture, we allow every smooth split loss:

F⁡(Σ):=ℓ⁡(Σv​u),Σ=(ΣuΣu​vΣv​uΣv).F(\Sigma):=\ell(\Sigma^{vu}),\qquad\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma^{u}&\Sigma^{uv}\\ \Sigma^{vu}&\Sigma^{v}\end{pmatrix}.

If E:=∇ℓ​(Σv​u)E:=\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu}), set

GE:=(0E⊤E0)∈𝔭J,𝔭J:={G∈𝕊m:G​J+J​G=0}.G_{E}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&E^{\top}\\ E&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{p}_{J},\qquad\mathfrak{p}_{J}:=\{G\in\mathbb{S}^{m}:GJ+JG=0\}.

The corresponding Bures vector field is

Xℓ​(Σ):=−(G∇ℓ​(Σv​u)​Σ+Σ​G∇ℓ​(Σv​u)).X_{\ell}(\Sigma):=-(G_{\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu})}\Sigma+\Sigma G_{\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu})}). (86)

We denote the resulting space of split Bures vector fields by

𝒳split:={Xℓ:ℓ∈C∞​(ℝdv×du)}.\mathcal{X}_{\rm split}:=\{X_{\ell}:\ell\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}})\}.

It is a real vector space. Its constant-gradient subspace is obtained from linear losses ℓE​(Σv​u):=⟨E,Σv​u⟩\ell_{E}(\Sigma^{vu}):=\left\langle E,\Sigma^{vu}\right\rangle:

𝒳lin:={XE:E∈ℝdv×du},XE​(Σ):=−(GE​Σ+Σ​GE).\mathcal{X}_{\rm lin}:=\{X_{E}:E\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}}\},\qquad X_{E}(\Sigma):=-(G_{E}\Sigma+\Sigma G_{E}).

D.2 Generated Lie algebra

Lie brackets reveal the directions generated by all split losses, which determine how many independent common laws can remain. Let

𝔬⁡(J):={A∈ℝm×m:A⊤​J+J​A=0}\mathfrak{o}(J):=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}:A^{\top}J+JA=0\}

be the Lie algebra of O⁡(du,dv)O(d_{u},d_{v}). For A∈𝔬⁡(J)A\in\mathfrak{o}(J), define the infinitesimal congruence field

ξA​(Σ):=−(A​Σ+Σ​A⊤).\xi_{A}(\Sigma):=-(A\Sigma+\Sigma A^{\top}).

Its flow is Σ⁡(t)=e−t​A​Σ​(0)​e−t​A⊤\Sigma(t)=e^{-tA}\Sigma(0)e^{-tA^{\top}}, so it is tangent to the O⁡(du,dv)O(d_{u},d_{v})-congruence orbit of Σ\Sigma. When A=GE∈𝔭JA=G_{E}\in\mathfrak{p}_{J}, ξA=XE\xi_{A}=X_{E}.

Proposition D.1 (Split fields generate 𝔬⁡(du,dv)\mathfrak{o}(d_{u},d_{v})).

With the bracket convention [X,Y]:=D​Y​[X]−D​X​[Y][X,Y]:=DY[X]-DX[Y], the map

A⟼ξAA\longmapsto\xi_{A}

is a Lie-algebra homomorphism:

[ξA,ξB]=ξ[A,B].[\xi_{A},\xi_{B}]=\xi_{[A,B]}.

Moreover,

Lie⁡(𝔭J)=𝔬⁡(J).\operatorname{Lie}(\mathfrak{p}_{J})=\mathfrak{o}(J).

Consequently the Lie algebra generated by 𝒳lin\mathcal{X}_{\rm lin}, the constant-gradient split Bures fields, is

{ξA:A∈𝔬⁡(J)}.\{\xi_{A}:A\in\mathfrak{o}(J)\}.
Proof.

The homomorphism identity follows by differentiating the linear vector fields ξA\xi_{A}. It remains to compute the matrix Lie algebra generated by 𝔭J\mathfrak{p}_{J}. For

GE=(0E⊤E0),GF=(0F⊤F0),G_{E}=\begin{pmatrix}0&E^{\top}\\ E&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad G_{F}=\begin{pmatrix}0&F^{\top}\\ F&0\end{pmatrix},

one has

[GE,GF]=(E⊤​F−F⊤​E00E​F⊤−F​E⊤).[G_{E},G_{F}]=\begin{pmatrix}E^{\top}F-F^{\top}E&0\\ 0&EF^{\top}-FE^{\top}\end{pmatrix}.

These brackets span the block-diagonal skew-symmetric algebra

𝔨J:={(A00D):A⊤=−A,D⊤=−D},\mathfrak{k}_{J}:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ 0&D\end{pmatrix}:A^{\top}=-A,\ D^{\top}=-D\right\},

by choosing E,FE,F supported on one common row or one common column. Since

𝔬⁡(J)=𝔨J⊕𝔭J,\mathfrak{o}(J)=\mathfrak{k}_{J}\oplus\mathfrak{p}_{J},

the generated Lie algebra is all of 𝔬⁡(J)\mathfrak{o}(J). ∎

Fields versus their generated distribution

The full space 𝒳split\mathcal{X}_{\rm split} contains nonlinear fields and is not identified with a finite-dimensional matrix Lie algebra. Each of its fields is a smooth, state-dependent linear combination of a basis of the XEX_{E}’s. Consequently all such fields and their brackets remain tangent to the same congruence orbits, while the constant-gradient fields already generate the whole orbit tangent space. It is this distribution that determines the common conservation laws.

D.3 Completeness of the spectral laws

The generated directions coincide with the tangent directions of covariance congruence orbits; their codimension gives the local law count. For a constant-gradient split Bures field, B:=J​ΣB:=J\Sigma satisfies

B˙=[GE,B].\dot{B}=[G_{E},B].

The trace powers ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} in (2) are therefore conserved. The next corollary states that, locally and generically, these are the only smooth covariance-level laws common to all split losses.

Let

Ωsimp:={Σ∈𝕊+⁣+m:J​Σ​ has simple spectrum}.\Omega_{\rm simp}:=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}:J\Sigma\text{ has simple spectrum}\}.
Corollary D.2 (Marcotte-style covariance-level completeness).

Let hh be a smooth function on an open subset of Ωsimp\Omega_{\rm simp}. If hh is conserved by every split Bures vector field XℓX_{\ell} of (86), then hh is locally a smooth function of the eigenvalues of J​ΣJ\Sigma, equivalently of

ℋ1​(Σ),…,ℋm​(Σ).\mathcal{H}_{1}(\Sigma),\ldots,\mathcal{H}_{m}(\Sigma).

These mm laws are functionally independent on Ωsimp\Omega_{\rm simp}. Thus the characteristic polynomial of J​ΣJ\Sigma gives a complete local/generic list of covariance-level mean-field conservation laws for the split two-layer linear architecture.

Proof.

It is enough to use the linear split losses. If XE​h=0X_{E}h=0 for every EE, then hh is also annihilated by all iterated Lie brackets of the XEX_{E}’s. By Proposition D.1,

d​h​(Σ)​[ξA​(Σ)]=0for all ​A∈𝔬⁡(J).\mathrm{d}h(\Sigma)[\xi_{A}(\Sigma)]=0\qquad\text{for all }A\in\mathfrak{o}(J).

Thus hh is constant on the connected pieces of the O⁡(du,dv)O(d_{u},d_{v})-congruence orbits.

The orbit invariants are exactly the eigenvalues of J​ΣJ\Sigma on Ωsimp\Omega_{\rm simp}. Indeed,

J⁡(Q​Σ​Q⊤)=Q−⁣⊤​(J​Σ)​Q⊤(Q⊤​J​Q=J),J(Q\Sigma Q^{\top})=Q^{-\top}(J\Sigma)Q^{\top}\qquad(Q^{\top}JQ=J),

so the spectrum is preserved. Conversely, for Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0, the matrix J​ΣJ\Sigma is similar to the symmetric matrix Σ1/2​J​Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}J\Sigma^{1/2}, hence has real nonzero eigenvalues with dud_{u} positive and dvd_{v} negative signs. On the simple-spectrum stratum its JJ-orthogonal eigenbasis can be locally normalized to a JJ-orthonormal basis, so equal locally ordered eigenvalues imply membership in the same local O⁡(du,dv)O(d_{u},d_{v})-orbit. Therefore any smooth orbit-constant function factors locally through the eigenvalues. Newton identities replace the eigenvalues by ℋ1,…,ℋm\mathcal{H}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{H}_{m}. More explicitly, for the locally ordered eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j},

∂ℋk∂λj=k​λjk−1,1≤k,j≤m.\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}_{k}}{\partial\lambda_{j}}=k\lambda_{j}^{k-1},\qquad 1\leq k,j\leq m.

This scaled Vandermonde matrix is invertible at distinct eigenvalues. The eigenvalues themselves vary independently by varying the diagonal covariance in a fixed normalized eigenbasis. Hence the spectral map has rank mm, and its local level sets have dimension m⁡(m+1)/2−m=m⁡(m−1)/2m(m+1)/2-m=m(m-1)/2, exactly the orbit dimension. ∎

For empirical covariances Σ=W​W⊤/n\Sigma=WW^{\top}/n with W=(UV)W=\binom{U}{V}, the finite-width Gram imbalance is

Γ:=V⊤​V−U⊤​U=−W⊤​J​W.\Gamma:=V^{\top}V-U^{\top}U=-W^{\top}JW.

The nonzero spectra of J​Σ=J​W​W⊤/nJ\Sigma=JWW^{\top}/n and −Γ/n=W⊤JW/n-\Gamma/n=W^{\top}JW/n coincide. Corollary D.2 is therefore the covariance quotient of the Marcotte–Gribonval–Peyré completeness theorem: the full labeled finite-width conservation data include the matrix Γ\Gamma, while the covariance-level law keeps only its spectrum.

D.4 A ReLU contrast

Homogeneity preserves a scalar balance beyond linear networks, but it does not give the same covariance closure or spectral family. For a two-layer ReLU or more generally one-homogeneous network, the characteristic equations associated with a potential v⊤​ψ​(u)v^{\top}\psi(u), with ψ\psi one-homogeneous and possibly time-dependent, have the form

u˙=−D​ψ​(u)⊤​v,v˙=−ψ⁡(u).\dot{u}=-D\psi(u)^{\top}v,\qquad\dot{v}=-\psi(u).

Euler’s identity D​ψ​(u)​u=ψ⁡(u)D\psi(u)u=\psi(u) gives

dd​t​(‖u‖2−‖v‖2)=0.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bigl(\left\lVert u\right\rVert^{2}-\left\lVert v\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)=0.

For ReLU this calculation is interpreted almost everywhere along the characteristics, with an activation-boundary convention satisfying Euler’s identity (for instance derivative zero at a zero preactivation). Thus the full mean-field flow preserves the pushforward distribution of ‖u‖2−‖v‖2\left\lVert u\right\rVert^{2}-\left\lVert v\right\rVert^{2}, and its covariance-level shadow is the total imbalance

∫(‖u‖2−‖v‖2)​𝑑μ​(u,v).\int\bigl(\left\lVert u\right\rVert^{2}-\left\lVert v\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(u,v).

Unlike the linear split case above, this ReLU statement is not obtained from a closed finite-dimensional Bures covariance equation; it is included only to highlight how much smaller the covariance-level conservation-law problem can be than the full particle-level one. No completeness claim for ReLU laws is made here.

Appendix E Intrinsic dynamics

Special conserved spectral values express some covariance blocks in terms of fewer variables. This appendix derives these exact reductions.

E.1 A two-point signed spectrum: hyperbolic isotropy

A special two-point spectrum determines the hidden covariance blocks from the predictor and therefore closes a smaller equation.

Definition E.1 (Hyperbolic isotropy).

For α>0\alpha>0, the hyperbolically isotropic (HI) leaf is

ℳα:={Σ⪰0:Σ​J​Σ=α2​J}.\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}:=\{\Sigma\succeq 0:\Sigma J\Sigma=\alpha^{2}J\}. (87)

The identity forces Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0 and is equivalent to (J​Σ)2=α2​Idm(J\Sigma)^{2}=\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{m}. The symmetric representative of J​ΣJ\Sigma then has dud_{u} eigenvalues +α+\alpha and dvd_{v} eigenvalues −α-\alpha; equivalently, ℋk=αk​(du+(−1)k​dv)\mathcal{H}_{k}=\alpha^{k}(d_{u}+(-1)^{k}d_{v}) for k=1,…,mk=1,\ldots,m. Spectral conservation proves invariance of ℳα\mathcal{M}_{\alpha} despite the repeated eigenvalues. Directly, the derivative of Σ​J​Σ\Sigma J\Sigma is −G⁡(Σ​J​Σ)−(Σ​J​Σ)​G-G(\Sigma J\Sigma)-(\Sigma J\Sigma)G, with constant solution α2​J\alpha^{2}J.

Proposition E.2 (Predictor-only intrinsic equation).

Every predictor Σv​u∈ℝdv×du\Sigma^{vu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{u}} has a unique covariance on ℳα\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}, given by

Σ=(((Σv​u)⊤​Σv​u+α2​Iddu)1/2(Σv​u)⊤Σv​u(Σv​u​(Σv​u)⊤+α2​Iddv)1/2).\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}((\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\Sigma^{vu}+\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}})^{1/2}&(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\\ \Sigma^{vu}&(\Sigma^{vu}(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}+\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{v}})^{1/2}\end{pmatrix}. (88)

On this leaf, the Bures dynamics close on the predictor:

Σ˙v​u=−E​((Σv​u)⊤​Σv​u+α2​Id)1/2−(Σv​u​(Σv​u)⊤+α2​Id)1/2​E,E:=∇ℓ​(Σv​u).\dot{\Sigma}^{vu}=-E((\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\Sigma^{vu}+\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id})^{1/2}-(\Sigma^{vu}(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}+\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id})^{1/2}E,\qquad E:=\nabla\ell(\Sigma^{vu}). (89)

For du=dv=1d_{u}=d_{v}=1, this is Σ˙v​u=−2​(Σv​u)2+α2​ℓ′​(Σv​u)\dot{\Sigma}^{vu}=-2\sqrt{(\Sigma^{vu})^{2}+\alpha^{2}}\,\ell^{\prime}(\Sigma^{vu}).

Proof.

Expanding (87) gives

(Σu)2−(Σv​u)⊤​Σv​u=α2​Id,(Σv)2−Σv​u​(Σv​u)⊤=α2​Id,Σv​u​Σu=Σv​Σv​u.(\Sigma^{u})^{2}-(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\Sigma^{vu}=\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id},\quad(\Sigma^{v})^{2}-\Sigma^{vu}(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}=\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id},\quad\Sigma^{vu}\Sigma^{u}=\Sigma^{v}\Sigma^{vu}.

Positivity selects the positive square roots. Conversely, an SVD proves the intertwining identity and gives eigenvalues α\alpha and σi2+α2±σi>0\sqrt{\sigma_{i}^{2}+\alpha^{2}}\pm\sigma_{i}>0, proving membership in ℳα\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}. Substituting the diagonal blocks into (24) gives the intrinsic equation. ∎

The same eigenvalue calculation gives the exact extremal envelopes

λmax​(Σ)=‖Σv​u‖op2+α2+‖Σv​u‖op,λmin​(Σ)=α2λmax​(Σ).\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)=\sqrt{\left\lVert\Sigma^{vu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}+\alpha^{2}}+\left\lVert\Sigma^{vu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\qquad\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}.

In the general convergence theorems this special spectral level has a+​(Σ0)=a−​(Σ0)=αa_{+}(\Sigma_{0})=a_{-}(\Sigma_{0})=\alpha. Thus its loss exponent is 4​α​κ4\alpha\kappa, and the GD contraction factor is 1−2​α​κ​τ1-\sqrt{2}\alpha\kappa\tau.

Finite-width form

The covariance constraint has an exact finite-width form that depends only on the product W​W⊤WW^{\top}. For Σ=W​W⊤/n\Sigma=WW^{\top}/n, condition (87) is W​W⊤​J​W​W⊤=n2​α2​JWW^{\top}JWW^{\top}=n^{2}\alpha^{2}J. In terms of U,VU,V, it reads

(UU⊤)2−UV⊤VU⊤=n2α2Iddu,(VV⊤)2−VU⊤UV⊤=n2α2Iddv,V​U⊤​U​U⊤=V​V⊤​V​U⊤.\begin{gathered}(UU^{\top})^{2}-UV^{\top}VU^{\top}=n^{2}\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{u}},\qquad(VV^{\top})^{2}-VU^{\top}UV^{\top}=n^{2}\alpha^{2}\mathrm{Id}_{d_{v}},\\ VU^{\top}UU^{\top}=VV^{\top}VU^{\top}.\end{gathered}

Any covariance in (88) admits empirical factors at every width n≥mn\geq m, for example W=n​Σ1/2​Q0W=\sqrt{n}\,\Sigma^{1/2}Q_{0} with Q0​Q0⊤=IdmQ_{0}Q_{0}^{\top}=\mathrm{Id}_{m}.

Comparison with relaxed balance

Marcotte et al. (2026, Theorem 3.8) derive intrinsic dynamics under a different condition, Γrb:=(V⊤​V−U⊤​U)/n=β​Idn\Gamma_{\rm rb}:=(V^{\top}V-U^{\top}U)/n=\beta\mathrm{Id}_{n}, on a full-column-rank stratum. It implies

(Σu)2+β​Σu=(Σv​u)⊤​Σv​u,(Σv)2−β​Σv=Σv​u​(Σv​u)⊤.(\Sigma^{u})^{2}+\beta\Sigma^{u}=(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\Sigma^{vu},\qquad(\Sigma^{v})^{2}-\beta\Sigma^{v}=\Sigma^{vu}(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}.

For β≠0\beta\neq 0, zero singular directions have ambiguous branches. Where both factors have full column rank, the range projectors Πu,Πv\Pi_{u},\Pi_{v} of (Σv​u)⊤,Σv​u(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top},\Sigma^{vu} select

Σu\displaystyle\Sigma^{u} =Πu​[−β2​Id+((Σv​u)⊤​Σv​u+β24​Id)1/2],\displaystyle=\Pi_{u}[-\tfrac{\beta}{2}\mathrm{Id}+((\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}\Sigma^{vu}+\tfrac{\beta^{2}}{4}\mathrm{Id})^{1/2}],
Σv\displaystyle\Sigma^{v} =Πv​[β2​Id+(Σv​u​(Σv​u)⊤+β24​Id)1/2].\displaystyle=\Pi_{v}[\tfrac{\beta}{2}\mathrm{Id}+(\Sigma^{vu}(\Sigma^{vu})^{\top}+\tfrac{\beta^{2}}{4}\mathrm{Id})^{1/2}].

If n=du=dvn=d_{u}=d_{v} and both factors are invertible, the projectors are identities and the predictor equation coincides with (89) for α=|β|/2\alpha=|\beta|/2. The leaves remain distinct: for β≠0\beta\neq 0, relaxed balance is equivalent to Σ​J​Σ=−β​Σ\Sigma J\Sigma=-\beta\Sigma, rank⁡Σ=n\operatorname{rank}\Sigma=n. Indeed a left inverse of W/nW/\sqrt{n} proves the converse. It forces n≤dvn\leq d_{v} if β>0\beta>0, and n≤dun\leq d_{u} if β<0\beta<0; positive HI instead has rank mm. For β=0\beta=0, positivity selects the unshifted square roots without a rank assumption, giving the boundary equation α=0\alpha=0, not a positive-definite initialization. Without the rank qualifications, relaxed balance does not ensure predictor closure: n=1,du=dv=2,U=0,V=e1n=1,d_{u}=d_{v}=2,U=0,V=e_{1} or e2e_{2} gives the same predictor and β=1\beta=1, but different predictor velocities for ℓ⁡(S):=‖S+Id2‖F2/2\ell(S):=\left\lVert S+\mathrm{Id}_{2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/2.

Remark E.3 (Conserved values do not generally close the predictor).

For du=dv=2d_{u}=d_{v}=2, take Σv​u=0\Sigma^{vu}=0, Σv=diag⁡(3,4)\Sigma^{v}=\operatorname{diag}(3,4), and Σu=diag⁡(1,2)\Sigma^{u}=\operatorname{diag}(1,2) or diag⁡(2,1)\operatorname{diag}(2,1). Both states have signed spectrum {1,2,−3,−4}\{1,2,-3,-4\}, hence the same spectral laws. For ℓ⁡(S):=‖S+e1​e1⊤‖F2/2\ell(S):=\left\lVert S+e_{1}e_{1}^{\top}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/2, their predictor velocities are −4​e1​e1⊤-4e_{1}e_{1}^{\top} and −5​e1​e1⊤-5e_{1}e_{1}^{\top}. The special two-point spectrum gives an algebraic graph unavailable at these general spectral values.

E.2 A single phase spectral scale: conformal symplectic isotropy

A special conformal spectral identity eliminates the velocity covariance within a positive-position chart of the phase flow.

Definition E.4 (Conformal symplectic isotropy).

A phase covariance is conformally symplectically isotropic (CSI) at scale θ≥0\theta\geq 0 if

Σ​Jc​Σ=θ2​Jc.\Sigma J_{\mathrm{c}}\Sigma=\theta^{2}J_{\mathrm{c}}. (90)

For θ>0\theta>0, this forces Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0 and is equivalent to Σ1/2​Jc​Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}J_{\mathrm{c}}\Sigma^{1/2} having mm copies of each eigenvalue +i​θ,−i​θ+i\theta,-i\theta. The renormalized trace powers in Proposition 5.1 are zero at odd orders and 2​m​(−1)k​θ02​k2m(-1)^{k}\theta_{0}^{2k} at order 2​k2k. Conformal transport preserves (90) with θt=e−γ​t​θ0\theta_{t}=e^{-\gamma t}\theta_{0}, including the singular boundary θ0=0\theta_{0}=0, which is specified algebraically, without diagonalizability.

Proposition E.5 (Reduced phase dynamics).

On the chart A:=Σ(u,v)≻0A:=\Sigma^{(u,v)}\succ 0, condition (90) is equivalent to

D=C=C⊤,Q=θ2​A−1,Ξ=A​C,Σ(p,q)=C​A​C+θ2​A−1.D=C=C^{\top},\qquad Q=\theta^{2}A^{-1},\qquad\Xi=AC,\quad\Sigma^{(p,q)}=CAC+\theta^{2}A^{-1}.

The reduced equations are

A˙=C​A+A​C,C˙=−G−γ​C−C2+θt2​A−2,θ˙t=−γ​θt.\dot{A}=CA+AC,\qquad\dot{C}=-G-\gamma C-C^{2}+\theta_{t}^{2}A^{-2},\qquad\dot{\theta}_{t}=-\gamma\theta_{t}. (91)

They use only the two symmetric matrices A,CA,C, with known scale θt\theta_{t}, instead of all blocks of the phase covariance.

Proof.

Substitute Ξ=A​D⊤\Xi=AD^{\top}, Σ(p,q)=D​A​D⊤+Q\Sigma^{(p,q)}=DAD^{\top}+Q. The upper-left block of (90) is A⁡(D−D⊤)​A=0A(D-D^{\top})A=0, forcing symmetry. The upper-right block then becomes A​Q=θ2​IdAQ=\theta^{2}\mathrm{Id}; the other blocks follow. Substitution in Proposition C.23 gives (91). This calculation includes θ=0\theta=0. ∎

White position and velocity blocks with Ξ0=0\Xi_{0}=0 give θ0=σv​u​σq​p\theta_{0}=\sigma_{vu}\sigma_{qp}. Zero velocity gives C0=0,θ0=0C_{0}=0,\theta_{0}=0, allowing any A0≻0A_{0}\succ 0. Neither choice is needed for convergence: the general theorem controls DD by energy even when it is nonsymmetric and QQ is independent.

Remark E.6 (What the reduced state still contains).

Even on CSI, the two cross blocks Σv​u,Σq​p\Sigma^{vu},\Sigma^{qp} do not generally form a closed state. With θ=1,C=0\theta=1,C=0, choose A=Id2A=\mathrm{Id}_{2} or 2​Id22\mathrm{Id}_{2} and Σ(p,q)=A−1\Sigma^{(p,q)}=A^{-1}. Both have Σv​u=Σq​p=Σ˙v​u=0\Sigma^{vu}=\Sigma^{qp}=\dot{\Sigma}^{vu}=0, yet Σ¨v​u=−2​E\ddot{\Sigma}^{vu}=-2E or −4​E-4E for the same nonzero scalar loss gradient. Thus the full position block remains part of the intrinsic variables.

Appendix F A nonquadratic example: smoothed Lasso

To illustrate the smooth PL loss class beyond quadratic objectives, we repeat the three experiments of Figure 2 with a smoothed entrywise ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty on the predictor:

ℓ⁡(S)=12​‖S−Steach‖F2+λ​∑i,j(Si​j2+δ2−δ),λ=0.1,δ=0.01.\ell(S)=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert S-S_{\rm teach}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{i,j}\Bigl(\sqrt{S_{ij}^{2}+\delta^{2}}-\delta\Bigr),\qquad\lambda=0.1,\quad\delta=0.01. (92)

The Hessian is diagonal, with entries 1+λ​δ2/(Si​j2+δ2)3/2∈[1,1+λ/δ]1+\lambda\delta^{2}/(S_{ij}^{2}+\delta^{2})^{3/2}\in[1,1+\lambda/\delta]. Thus ℓ\ell is globally 11-strongly convex and satisfies Assumption 1.1 with κ=1\kappa=1 and L=11L=11. The penalty acts on SS, not separately on the factors, so the covariance closure and spectral conservation laws apply without modification.
